content: Fire ants, also known as red ants, are stinging ants with over 280 species distributed globally. They are also referred to by various names, such as Ginger Ants and Tropical Fire Ants in English, aka-kami-ari in Japanese, and Feuerameise in German. Appearance The bodies of fire ants, like all insects, are divided into three sections: the head, thorax, and abdomen. They possess three pairs of legs and a pair of antennae. Fire ants are distinguishable by their copper-brown head and body, contrasted with a darker abdomen. They exhibit polymorphism, meaning ants of different sizes can coexist within the same nest. Behavior Fire ant colonies typically construct large mounds in open areas and primarily feed on young plants, seeds, and occasionally small insects like crickets. They are known to attack and kill small animals. Unlike many other ants that bite and spray acid on wounds, fire ants bite to secure their grip and then sting using their abdomen, injecting a toxic alkaloid venom called solenopsin, a compound from the piperidine class. This venom causes a painful sting, often described as a burning sensation, which is the origin of their name. For sensitive individuals, the sting can have severe or even fatal consequences. The venom also exhibits insecticidal and antibiotic properties, and nurse worker ants are known to spray their brood with venom to protect them from microorganisms. Fire ants typically nest in soil, often near moist areas such as riverbanks, pond edges, watered lawns, and highway edges. Their nests are often hidden under objects like timber, logs, rocks, pavers, or bricks. In the absence of cover, they construct dome-shaped mounds, usually found in open spaces like fields, parks, and lawns. Colonies are founded by single or small groups of queens, and even if only one queen survives, the colony can grow to thousands of individuals within a month. Some colonies are polygynous, meaning they have multiple queens. In certain regions, such as the Klang Valley in Malaysia, fire ants build nests by folding leaves and sealing them with a sticky white excretion, which also serves to protect the queen and eggs. Fire ants are highly defensive of their nests and will aggressively attack intruders. Even the slightest disturbance can provoke a swarm of ants to emerge in a fury. Roles in the Colony Queens: The queen is typically the largest individual in the colony and is primarily responsible for reproduction. A queen can live for 6–7 years and produce up to 1,500 eggs per day. Many fire ant colonies have more than one queen. Males: Male ants mate with the queen to facilitate egg production. They also defend the queen in the event of an attack or structural damage to the colony. Workers: Worker ants are sterile females responsible for building and repairing the nest, caring for the young, defending the colony, and feeding both young and adult ants. Introduced Species While most fire ant species are not invasive or harmful to humans, Solenopsis invicta, commonly known as the Red Imported Fire Ant (RIFA), is a significant invasive pest in many parts of the world, including the United States, Australia, the Philippines, China, and Taiwan. RIFA was accidentally introduced to the United States via a South American cargo ship that arrived at an Alabama port in 1918. It now infests much of the southern and southwestern United States. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) estimates that over $5 billion is spent annually on medical treatment, damage repair, and control efforts in RIFA-infested areas. Additionally, these ants cause approximately $750 million in annual agricultural damage, including veterinary bills, livestock losses, and crop destruction. Since September 2004, Taiwan has also been severely affected by RIFA. Efforts to control or eradicate the species are ongoing in the U.S., Taiwan, and Australia, but only Australia has achieved significant success, eradicating 99% of fire ants in South East Queensland through an intensive program costing A$175 million as of February 2007. Symptoms and First Aid The venom from a fire ant sting causes a painful, stinging sensation and swelling, which develops into a bump. This bump often forms a white pustule that can become infected. The pustules are unsightly and uncomfortable, and if the bite sites become infected, they may leave scars. Some individuals are allergic to the venom and may experience anaphylaxis, a life-threatening allergic reaction requiring immediate medical attention. Antihistamines or topical corticosteroids can help alleviate itching. First aid for fire ant stings includes: External treatments: Applying a topical steroid cream (e.g., hydrocortisone) or one containing aloe vera. Oral medications: Taking antihistamines. Patients experiencing severe or life-threatening allergic reactions should seek emergency medical care immediately, as these reactions can be fatal. Other Names In Spanish, fire ants are called hormiga colorada/roja (red ant) or hormiga brava (fierce ant). In Puerto Rico, a native, small, and slow-moving type of fire ant is known as abayarde. In Portuguese, they are referred to as formiga de fogo (fire ant) or formiga lava-pé (wash foot ant). Species The list of fire ant species is incomplete.
